name: Vitamin B12 and folate tests explained
summary: B12 and folate blood tests help find the cause of deficiency anaemia, but a B12 result alone can miss cases, so symptoms matter too.
keyPoints: Vitamin B12 and folate deficiency can both cause anaemia in which the body makes abnormally large red blood cells.
A GP combines symptoms with blood tests that check the level of vitamin B12 and of folate.
A UK clinical guideline says a B12 blood test is not completely reliable, so two tests are requested when deficiency is suspected.
B12 deficiency is usually treated with injections of hydroxocobalamin, and folate deficiency with folic acid tablets.

body.heading: What are vitamin B12 and folate deficiency anaemia?
body.body: Vitamin B12 and folate are both needed to make healthy red blood cells. When either is lacking, the body can make abnormally large red blood cells that do not work as they should. This is called vitamin B12 or folate deficiency anaemia.

body.heading: What symptoms can it cause?
body.body: The NHS lists tiredness along with numbness, muscle weakness, psychological problems, problems with balance and coordination, pins and needles and incontinence. Folate deficiency anaemia adds symptoms such as breathlessness, pale skin and palpitations. Some effects of B12 deficiency can appear without anaemia and without a low blood level. Mouth ulcers, a sore red tongue and problems with vision or memory are also listed.

body.heading: How is it diagnosed?
body.body: A GP typically combines symptoms with blood tests. The blood tests check the level of vitamin B12 and the level of folate in the blood. A UK clinical guideline notes that a vitamin B12 blood test is not completely reliable and asks for two tests when deficiency is suspected. The same guideline says routine screening for B12 deficiency is not appropriate. The NHS says a GP should be involved when the cause is unclear, in pregnancy, or when symptoms suggest the nervous system is affected.

body.heading: What causes deficiency?
body.body: The NHS says pernicious anaemia is the most common cause of vitamin B12 deficiency in the UK. Pernicious anaemia is an autoimmune condition that affects the stomach, so B12 from food is not absorbed. Lack of B12 from the diet is uncommon, but it can happen with a vegan diet that includes no supplements or fortified foods. Some medicines, including proton pump inhibitors and metformin, can reduce B12 levels. Folate deficiency can be linked to some medicines, such as certain anticonvulsants and methotrexate.

body.heading: How is it treated?
body.body: B12 deficiency anaemia is usually treated with injections of vitamin B12, called hydroxocobalamin. When the cause is diet, treatment may be daily B12 tablets instead. Folate deficiency is usually treated with folic acid tablets. Clinicians check B12 status first, because folic acid can mask a vitamin B12 deficiency. Follow-up blood tests check that treatment is working. A GP appointment is the route for symptoms such as numbness, pins and needles or problems with balance.
